title: Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator
creator: Twin City Fan
subject: Fans and air movement
description: Four fixed challenges ask the learner to calculate air velocity, airflow or minimum flow area for rectangular and round ducts using Q = V x A, checked within 2 percent with step-by-step feedback; a free mode then shows how velocity changes with duct size at fixed CFM.

educational.topic: Airflow, velocity and flow area in ducts (Q = V x A)
learningObjectives: Calculate air velocity, airflow volume or required flow area from the other two quantities for rectangular and round ducts, to within 2 percent of the model value.
prerequisites: Airflow volume in cubic feet per minute (CFM)
Air velocity in feet per minute
The equation Q = V x A
Converting duct dimensions in inches to square feet

equations: Round A = pi x D^2 / 576 ft^2
assumptions: Velocity is the average velocity over the full duct cross-section
Duct dimensions are inside dimensions in inches
simulationModel.dataProvenance: Challenge 1 is the chapter's machine-shop worked example; challenges 2-4 are illustrative values and are labeled as such in the sim.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Committed-answer practice problems with immediate diagnostic feedback, followed by free exploration
keyQuestions: Why must duct dimensions in inches be divided by 144 before dividing CFM by area?
Does a bigger duct move more air when the fan airflow is unchanged?
Is a round duct of diameter D the same area as a square duct of side D?
commonMisconceptions: Velocity can be found by dividing CFM by the duct dimensions in inches without converting to square feet.
A bigger duct moves more air at the same fan airflow; in fact the CFM is the same and only the velocity drops.
A round duct of diameter D has the same area as a square duct of side D.
assessmentOpportunities: Mastery: 4 of 4 challenges correct within 2 percent, at most two attempts each
Free exploration is not evidence of mastery
